evidence.supportingExcerpt: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

points.requirement: **1. Leave the node and hear the call.** After priming, effector T cells change the receptors on their surface. They leave the lymph node, enter the blood and now carry chemokine receptors such as CXCR3. Tissues that are inflamed release chemokines such as CXCL9 and CXCL10, which bind CXCR3. In human melanoma metastases, six chemokines including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10 were expressed mainly in tumors that contained T cells ([Harlin et al., 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19293190/)).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Harlin found six chemokines, including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10, preferentially in T-cell-containing human melanoma metastases, with supporting migration experiments. In melanoma models, Mikucki found that CXCR3 supported intravascular arrest and extravasation of transferred CD8 effectors. These findings identify defined recruitment and vascular dependencies, not a universal explanation for every abnormal vessel. Spranger’s human melanoma association and mouse experiments connected tumour WNT/beta-catenin activity with deficient dendritic-cell recruitment and absent T-cell infiltration, a desert-like problem rather than necessarily an excluded rim. In their 2015 commentary on the mouse experiments, Spranger and Gajewski describe reduced CCL4 expression and failed recruitment of Batf3-lineage dendritic cells. This is a defined melanoma mechanism, not a universal explanation for every excluded tissue pattern.

points.requirement: **2. Grip the vessel wall and exit.** A T cell in a fast-flowing vessel first rolls along the wall, then sticks firmly using adhesion molecules, then squeezes between the lining cells ([Slaney et al., 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25477332/)). points.requirement: **3. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Dendritic cells acquire material from their surroundings or make antigen themselves, process proteins and display fragments on HLA molecules, where a matching T-cell receptor can recognise a peptide and HLA pair. Cross-presentation is the route that places acquired material on class I, and class II presentation, usually of acquired proteins to CD4 T cells, is a separate route. They are a family of subsets with overlapping jobs. Conventional type 1 cells (cDC1) are particularly important for cross-presentation: mice lacking the transcription factor Batf3 lost CD8-alpha-positive dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they rejected highly immunogenic tumours less well (Hildner et al., 2008). Human CD141-positive dendritic cells, activated with poly I:C, cross-presented soluble antigen and antigen from necrotic virus-infected cells better than CD1c-positive cells (Jongbloed et al., 2010). Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). The same review describes conventional cells as inducing immunity to foreign antigens and enforcing tolerance to self-antigens, and migration-linked maturation as raising MHC class II and costimulatory molecules, with cytokine production added when migration follows inflammation. In mice, antigen delivered to dendritic cells in the steady state led to brief T-cell activation followed by loss and unresponsiveness of the T cells, and adding an anti-CD40 antibody changed the outcome to prolonged activation (Hawiger et al., 2001). For conventional type 2 cells, a review of dendritic cells in T-cell programming reported that they were most often found to be required for CD4 T-cell priming in mice, with T helper 1 differentiation as an exception in which type 1 cells were often required, and noted that type 2 cells can be difficult to distinguish from monocyte-derived cells because markers overlap (Eisenbarth, 2019); another review said that specific depletion of type 2 cells was still needed to confirm their unique role in priming CD4 T cells (Durai and Murphy, 2016). Single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes, including a population that resembles plasmacytoid cells but potently activates T cells, so one positive marker is weaker evidence than a supported subset assignment (Villani et al., 2017).

points.requirement: - [Lymph nodes and lymphatics](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/the-immune-system/lymph-nodes-and-lymphatics): where T cells are primed.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). evidence.supportingExcerpt: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

points.requirement: **1. Leave the node and hear the call.** After priming, effector T cells change the receptors on their surface. They leave the lymph node, enter the blood and now carry chemokine receptors such as CXCR3. Tissues that are inflamed release chemokines such as CXCL9 and CXCL10, which bind CXCR3. In human melanoma metastases, six chemokines including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10 were expressed mainly in tumors that contained T cells ([Harlin et al., 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19293190/)).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Harlin found six chemokines, including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10, preferentially in T-cell-containing human melanoma metastases, with supporting migration experiments. In melanoma models, Mikucki found that CXCR3 supported intravascular arrest and extravasation of transferred CD8 effectors. These findings identify defined recruitment and vascular dependencies, not a universal explanation for every abnormal vessel. Spranger’s human melanoma association and mouse experiments connected tumour WNT/beta-catenin activity with deficient dendritic-cell recruitment and absent T-cell infiltration, a desert-like problem rather than necessarily an excluded rim. In their 2015 commentary on the mouse experiments, Spranger and Gajewski describe reduced CCL4 expression and failed recruitment of Batf3-lineage dendritic cells. This is a defined melanoma mechanism, not a universal explanation for every excluded tissue pattern.

points.requirement: **2. Grip the vessel wall and exit.** A T cell in a fast-flowing vessel first rolls along the wall, then sticks firmly using adhesion molecules, then squeezes between the lining cells ([Slaney et al., 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25477332/)). Tumor vessels are often leaky and disorganized, and their lining may show little of the adhesion molecules intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1). In mouse and human melanoma models, CXCR3 signaling was needed for transferred CD8 T cells to stick inside tumor vessels and leave them ([Mikucki et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26109379/)).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Reduced endothelial adhesion molecules have been measured in defined tumour settings. Griffioen and colleagues found lower vascular ICAM-1 in renal-cell carcinoma than in healthy-tissue endothelial comparators. In cultured endothelial cells, basic fibroblast growth factor first increased and later decreased ICAM-1, with corresponding changes in leukocyte adhesion. points.requirement: **3. Cross the stroma.** Outside the vessel lies the stroma: [fibroblasts](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/tumor-microenvironment/cancer-associated-fibroblasts-and-stroma), collagen and other [extracellular matrix](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/tumor-microenvironment/extracellular-matrix). In live slices of human lung tumors, T cells moved freely in loose matrix, stalled in dense matrix and tracked along aligned fibers that steered them around cancer-cell islands. Digesting collagen let more T cells reach cancer cells ([Salmon et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22293174/)).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In viable human lung-tumour slices, Salmon observed better T-cell movement in loose matrix, restricted movement in dense aligned matrix and increased cancer-cell contact after collagenase. Mariathasan associated stromal fibroblast TGF-beta signalling, exclusion and atezolizumab non-response in metastatic urothelial cancer; combined TGF-beta and PD-L1 blockade improved penetration and regression in mice. Peranzoni linked long macrophage-CD8 contacts and poor motility to exclusion in human lung squamous cancers, then used macrophage-directed treatment in mice to improve tumour-islet access. None of these model interventions establishes a beneficial breast-cancer regimen.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Reduced endothelial adhesion molecules have been measured in defined tumour settings. Griffioen and colleagues found lower vascular ICAM-1 in renal-cell carcinoma than in healthy-tissue endothelial comparators. In cultured endothelial cells, basic fibroblast growth factor first increased and later decreased ICAM-1, with corresponding changes in leukocyte adhesion. These studies support a candidate vascular entry barrier, not its frequency in every cancer or a universal effect of angiogenic factors. points.requirement: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) shows all three patterns. In 681 TNBCs, Hammerl and colleagues found that excluded tumors carried collagen deposits and TGF-β and blood-vessel growth signaling. "Ignored" tumors, with few T cells, showed either many CD163-positive myeloid cells (a macrophage type) or WNT pathway activity. Inflamed tumors had more CLEC9A-positive dendritic cells, the subtype that specializes in priming CD8 T cells. In a phase II trial of an anti-PD-1 drug in metastatic TNBC, the inflamed pattern went with response and the other two with resistance ([Hammerl et al., 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34580291/)).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Hammerl’s spatial analysis of 681 TNBCs distinguished excluded, ignored and inflamed groups. Excluded samples showed collagen-10 deposits and TGF-beta/VEGF programmes; ignored samples showed either dense CD163-positive myeloid cells or WNT/PPAR-gamma programmes. Inflamed samples had more CLEC9A-positive dendritic cells, a population association rather than a direct measurement of successful priming. The classifier also associated with anti-PD-1 response in a metastatic-TNBC phase-II trial. Gruosso separately associated stroma-restricted CD8 cells and stromal PD-L1 with poorer outcome. These associations do not prove the observed barrier caused resistance or that its removal helps a particular patient.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Dendritic cells acquire material from their surroundings or make antigen themselves, process proteins and display fragments on HLA molecules, where a matching T-cell receptor can recognise a peptide and HLA pair. Cross-presentation is the route that places acquired material on class I, and class II presentation, usually of acquired proteins to CD4 T cells, is a separate route. They are a family of subsets with overlapping jobs. Conventional type 1 cells (cDC1) are particularly important for cross-presentation: mice lacking the transcription factor Batf3 lost CD8-alpha-positive dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they rejected highly immunogenic tumours less well (Hildner et al., 2008). Human CD141-positive dendritic cells, activated with poly I:C, cross-presented soluble antigen and antigen from necrotic virus-infected cells better than CD1c-positive cells (Jongbloed et al., 2010). Conventional type 2 cells are usually studied for class II presentation to CD4 T cells, and plasmacytoid cells for type I interferon responses. In a review, plasmacytoid cells are described as producing large amounts of interferon alpha, while the contribution of CD11b-positive conventional cells to CD4 T-cell priming in vivo was still described as to be determined (Merad et al., 2013). The same review describes conventional cells as inducing immunity to foreign antigens and enforcing tolerance to self-antigens, and migration-linked maturation as raising MHC class II and costimulatory molecules, with cytokine production added when migration follows inflammation. In mice, antigen delivered to dendritic cells in the steady state led to brief T-cell activation followed by loss and unresponsiveness of the T cells, and adding an anti-CD40 antibody changed the outcome to prolonged activation (Hawiger et al., 2001). For conventional type 2 cells, a review of dendritic cells in T-cell programming reported that they were most often found to be required for CD4 T-cell priming in mice, with T helper 1 differentiation as an exception in which type 1 cells were often required, and noted that type 2 cells can be difficult to distinguish from monocyte-derived cells because markers overlap (Eisenbarth, 2019); another review said that specific depletion of type 2 cells was still needed to confirm their unique role in priming CD4 T cells (Durai and Murphy, 2016). Single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes, including a population that resembles plasmacytoid cells but potently activates T cells, so one positive marker is weaker evidence than a supported subset assignment (Villani et al., 2017).

points.requirement: - **Calling an excluded tumor cold.** The T cells are close by; the barrier is the problem, not their absence.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In viable human lung-tumour slices, Salmon observed better T-cell movement in loose matrix, restricted movement in dense aligned matrix and increased cancer-cell contact after collagenase. Peranzoni linked long macrophage-CD8 contacts and poor motility to exclusion in human lung squamous cancers, then used macrophage-directed treatment in mice to improve tumour-islet access. None of these model interventions establishes a beneficial breast-cancer regimen.
